latest_nl_proof: Assume for contradiction that Circle(O,r) contains three distinct points A, B, C whose color is different from f(O). Since f takes values only in {red,green}, all three of A, B, C must then have the same color, namely the color opposite to f(O). Thus f(A)=f(B)=f(C) and f(A) != f(O). We first show that A, B, C are noncollinear. Indeed, let l be any line, and let D be the foot of the perpendicular from O to l. For any point X on l, the right triangle ODX gives OX^2 = OD^2 + DX^2. Hence the condition X in Circle(O,r), i.e. OX = r, is equivalent to DX^2 = r^2 - OD^2, which has at most two solutions on the line l. So a line meets Circle(O,r) in at most two points. Therefore three distinct points on Circle(O,r) cannot be collinear, and A, B, C are noncollinear. Next, because OA=OB=r, the point O is equidistant from A and B, so O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB. Likewise, OA=OC=r, so O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AC. Since A, B, C are noncollinear, their circumcenter is, by definition, the unique intersection point of these two perpendicular bisectors. Therefore circumcenter(A,B,C)=O. Now apply the hypothesis of the lemma to the noncollinear monochromatic triple A, B, C. We get f(circumcenter(A,B,C)) = f(A). Since circumcenter(A,B,C)=O, this says f(O)=f(A), contradicting f(A) != f(O). This contradiction shows that Circle(O,r) cannot contain three distinct points whose color is different from f(O). Hence it contains at most two such points. In particular, there do not exist three distinct points A, B, C on Circle(O,r) with f(A)=f(B)=f(C) != f(O).
role_in_parent: Provides the bound that on the large circle centered at O, among the ten support points at most two can have the opposite color.
statement_nl: Let f : R^2 -> {red,green} be a coloring with the following property: for every noncollinear triple A,B,C in R^2, if f(A)=f(B)=f(C), then f(circumcenter(A,B,C))=f(A). Fix a point O in R^2 and a real number r>0. Then the circle Circle(O,r) contains at most two points whose color is different from f(O). Equivalently, there do not exist three distinct points A,B,C on Circle(O,r) with f(A)=f(B)=f(C) != f(O).

domain_restrictions: f is a function from R^2 to the two-element set {red,green}
P(f) quantifies only over noncollinear triples (circumcenter is only asserted/used for noncollinear triples)
O is any point in R^2 and r is any strictly positive real number
In the conclusion A,B,C (if existentially asserted) are required to be distinct and lie on Circle(O,r)
Circumcenter(A,B,C) is meaningful only for noncollinear A,B,C
statement_semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every function f: R^2 -> {red,green} satisfying P(f) (where P(f) := for all noncollinear A,B,C in R^2, if f(A)=f(B)=f(C) then f(circumcenter(A,B,C))=f(A)), for every O in R^2 and every r>0 it holds that there do not exist three distinct points A,B,C in Circle(O,r) with f(A)=f(B)=f(C) and f(A) != f(O). Equivalently: for every such f,O,r, the set {X in Circle(O,r) : f(X) != f(O)} has cardinality at most 2.
quantifier_order: forall f: (R^2 -> {red,green}) such that P(f) holds
where P(f) is: forall noncollinear A,B,C in R^2, (f(A)=f(B)=f(C) implies f(circumcenter(A,B,C))=f(A))
forall r in R with r>0
conclusion: not (exists distinct A,B,C in Circle(O,r) with f(A)=f(B)=f(C) and f(A) != f(O))

variables.name: f
variables.role: coloring function f: R^2 -> {red,green} (global hypothesis variable)

variables.name: O
variables.role: center of circle (arbitrary fixed point in conclusion)

variables.name: A
variables.role: generic point (used both in hypothesis about triples and as a potential point on the circle in the conclusion)

variables.domain: R^2 (defined only when A,B,C are noncollinear)
variables.name: circumcenter(A,B,C)
variables.role: circumcenter of the triangle ABC (used in the property P of f)

variables.name: Circle(O,r)
variables.role: the geometric circle {X in R^2 : dist(X,O)=r} used in the conclusion

witness_dependencies: The (negated) existential in the conclusion, if it were to hold, would provide A,B,C that depend on f, O, r; i.e. any witness triple (A,B,C) would be a function of (f,O,r)
There is no global existential witness in the statement as given; the final claim is a universal-negative (¬∃) for each fixed f,O,r
